extracted.intended_audience: researchers, meta-analysts, and journal editors studying peer-review reliability and methods
extracted.subtask_description: Meta-analytic evaluation of inter-rater reliability (IRR) in journal peer reviews, including statistical synthesis (multilevel models) and investigation of determinants (covariates) that explain study-to-study variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (IRR) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: IRR is defined as 'the extent to which two or more independent reviews of the same scientific document agree' (Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRR is the target quantity to be estimated and interpreted; the paper reports low levels (mean ICC/r ≈ .34, mean Cohen's Kappa ≈ .17) and treats IRR as an indicator of agreement among reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability coefficients (Cohen's Kappa, ICC, Pearson r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all primary studies provided one or more of Cohen's Kappa, intra-class correlation (ICC), and Pearson product-moment correlation (r) as IRR estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ICC when available (measures absolute consensus and consistency). r can substantially overestimate IRR except when reviewer ratings have identical means/variances. For pooled analyses, the square root of ICC was used as a correlation analogue and Fisher Z-transformed correlations (and corresponding SEs) were used for meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria for meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Include studies that report both a reliability coefficient (ICC, r, or Cohen's Kappa) and the number of manuscripts on which the coefficient was based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different coefficients exist for the same sample, include ICCs preferentially; exclude studies that report neither ICC, r, nor Kappa or that lack manuscript counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilevel (three-level) meta-analysis model
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multilevel models (three-level: manuscript, sample, study) to summarize reliabilities and to account for dependence among multiple coefficients reported by the same study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multilevel models simultaneously estimate overall reliability and between-study variability, and they correct dependence among coefficients (e.g., multiple samples within one study), avoiding distorted SE estimates that arise if independence is (incorrectly) assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed effects vs random effects models
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed effects models assume one common IRR for all included studies; random effects models estimate the average of a distribution of reliabilities, allowing true effect sizes to vary across studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed effects generalize only to included studies; random effects generalize to a super-population. Choice affects standard errors (random effects incorporate between-study variability) and interpretation of pooled estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Number of manuscripts (sample size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of manuscripts used to compute each reliability coefficient (entered divided by 100 in regressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger sample sizes were associated with smaller reported IRR coefficients (regression coefficient −.03 per 100 manuscripts). This pattern indicates publication bias: small studies reporting high IRR are more likely to be published. Include sample size as a covariate to control for this bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Method used to calculate IRR (ICC vs r)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statistical method (ICC or r) used to compute IRR in primary studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different methods produce different magnitudes (r may overestimate). To combine ICC and r in one analysis, take the square root of ICC to create a correlation analogue and apply Fisher Z-transformation for meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific discipline of the study (economics/law; natural sciences; medical sciences; social sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a categorical covariate (dummy-coded) to test whether discipline explains IRR differences. The paper found no significant discipline effect in these analyses, but discipline remains a theoretical factor to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Object of appraisal (paper vs abstract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the unit being reviewed was a full paper (research article/short communication) or an abstract (e.g., conference abstract).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts may yield different levels of agreement than full papers (hypothesized to show relatively higher disagreement). Include as a categorical covariate (paper vs abstract) to test this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Cohort (time period)
rubrics_metrics.description: The period on which primary-study data are based (e.g., 1950–1979, 1980–1989, 1990–1999, 2000–2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohort tests whether IRR has changed over time; include as categorical covariate and handle missing/unknown as an explicit category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Blinding (single vs double)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of masking used in peer review (single-blind, double-blind, unknown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesized that double-blind increases IRR by reducing bias; empirical finding here: no significant blinding effect. Note practical masking difficulties (reviewers often identify authors). Include blinding as a covariate and code unknown when not reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression covariate: Rating system (categorical vs metric; reported vs unknown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type and reporting of the rating/evaluation system used by reviewers (classified as categorical if ≤9 categories, metric if >9 categories; or unknown if not reported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the rating system is reported is an indicator of study quality. Studies that reported the rating system tended to show smaller IRR coefficients; failure to mention the rating system should be viewed as an indication of lower study quality. Include rating system (and whether reported) as covariate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification rule for rating scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating systems are classified as categorical if they have nine or fewer categories, and as metric if they have more than nine categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational rule was used in coding primary studies for the regression analyses and affects categorization in meta-regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical practices for meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Fisher Z-transformed correlations and corresponding standard errors; weight studies by inverse standard error; use mixed/multilevel models (SAS PROC MIXED in this study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighting gives more influence to studies with larger sample sizes (smaller SE). Multilevel models permit estimation of variance components at different levels; compare models using likelihood tests and BIC. Impute or code missing categorical covariates as 'unknown' to preserve sample size in meta-regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple coefficients per study (dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single study reports multiple reliability coefficients (different journals/cohorts), coefficients are not independent and must be modeled as nested (coefficients within samples within studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a multilevel approach (three-level model) to account for within-study dependence; this reduces biased SEs and provides more accurate variance component estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance for Cohen's Kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa interpretation per Landis & Koch: example given that mean Kappa ≈ .17 indicates 'slight' IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established interpretive guidelines (Landis & Koch) to qualify Kappa magnitudes; report CIs and context for practical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standards & recommended quality features for primary studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary studies should report reliability coefficients and the number of manuscripts; they should describe the evaluation sheet/rating system for reviewers in detail and use large sample sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis is more reliable when primary studies provide detailed rating-system information and large samples. Omission of rating-system details or small samples undermines credibility and contributes to publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to improve IRR (reader system; number of reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to increase IRR include a reader trial system (a small number of expert readers reviewing all proposals in a subdiscipline) and using three or four reviewers rather than two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reader systems produced much higher single-rater reliabilities (example: average 4.3 readers produced IRR ≈ .88 for researcher ratings). Use of more reviewers can reduce decision errors; however trade-offs with cost and reviewer selection must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration that high agreement may not always be desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much agreement might indicate the review process is not working well (redundant reviewers, lack of diverse perspectives); low IRR can reflect legitimate diversity of competent views at the research frontier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing and evaluating peer review, balance desired reliability with reviewer diversity and validity; selecting reviewers for complementarity may lower IRR but increase validity.
